title: Eight Weeks of Clinical Clerkship at Lund University
paragraphs: Nice to meet you. I am 吉田奈央, a sixth-year student in the Department of Medicine of the Nagoya University School of Medicine. Thanks to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, I was able to finish a two-month clerkship at Lund University. As this was the first clerkship dispatch abroad since the COVID-19 pandemic, I sincerely thank everyone who made various efforts for it.

In the clerkship at Lund University, I took part in hand surgery and medical oncology, and in emergency medicine for only one week. The hospital where I did my clerkship was a public hospital in the Skåne region of southern Sweden. Sweden has a low population density, and even the whole Skåne region, which is relatively populous, has a smaller population than the city of Nagoya. The hospital system is also increasingly centralized: hand surgery exists only in Malmö, the only place in the Skåne region; medical oncology is mainly at the hospitals in Lund and Malmö, and groups with many patients, such as gastrointestinal tumors, had clinical departments in two other places as well. In addition, public hospitals make up most of the hospitals in Sweden, and there the people can receive medical care through very generous insurance. On the other hand, in the small number of private hospitals, with exceptions, treatment is at one's own expense, but in exchange, unlike public hospitals, they make up for the weaknesses of public facilities, such as short waiting times until surgery and providing care on weekends.

Next, in medical oncology, I observed outpatient clinics of various groups by organ and the wards, and also took part in breast cancer surgery. The outpatient clinic had around 10 patients a day, with a generous appointment slot of 30 to 45 minutes per patient, and the schedule rarely ran over. The number of doctors is by no means large, so when I asked why they could take time like this, a doctor told me that medical oncology regularly follows patients for a fixed period determined by tumor type and prognosis, but after that period the patient is sent to the general practitioner in charge. Even so, there is a shortage of staff, and the workload of general practitioners has apparently become greater than others. As for the treatments being given, of course the basic cancer treatment regimens did not differ greatly even compared with Japanese guidelines, but it was very interesting to learn the latest evidence and clinical trials that Lund University is working on. In breast cancer surgery, the procedure differed slightly from that performed in Japan, and it was also fun to think about whether this is due to differences in physique among countries, differences in preferred surgical technique, the time required for pathological diagnosis and so on. During outpatient clinics, patients and doctors basically speak in Swedish, but as I wrote earlier, since there was leeway in outpatient time, I could receive sufficient explanations in between and ask various questions. In addition, since lymph node, abdominal and breast palpation examinations and so on were performed on almost all patients, I was allowed to do them each time after the doctor. For young patients they sometimes held the clinic in English, for which I was very grateful. On the last day I was allowed to give one case presentation; I was given a case of breast cancer, the tumor I am most interested in, and prepared it while translating the chart into English with Google Translate.

In Japan medical oncology does not exist in many facilities, but I learned its high degree of specialization, in the variety of anticancer drugs, combinations and administration schedules and in responding to side effects. After finishing the clerkship, I came to think all the more that in Japan too, a movement to separate the surgery that removes tumors from the medical oncology that provides drug therapy before and after surgery will probably advance in the future.

Finally, about emergency medicine. Emergency care runs on a three-shift system, from 8:00 to 15:00, 15:00 to 22:00, and 22:00 to 8:00 the next day, and students did the clerkship in one of these slots plus extra time. I mainly did the clerkship from 8:00 to around 17:00, and once from 2:00 to 9:00. What impressed me most was that the Lund University students actively talked to patients, and during the waiting time until the doctor went to the patient and responded, they took the history and did the physical examination themselves, and even wrote the chart while thinking about the differential diagnosis and what to do next. I too did this with young patients who could speak English or with Lund University students interpreting for me, but actual patients often have atypical symptoms, and after reporting to the doctor I was always learning "so it was this disease." It was also interesting that, to prevent unnecessary and non-urgent visits to the emergency department, the reception nurse looks at the patient's condition and recommends coming another day, and the paramedics can ask a doctor's opinion from the scene and decline transport by ambulance. Waiting times in the emergency outpatient department are basically very long, and although the goal is to be able to talk with a doctor within three hours after the patient arrives, I heard that even that is not always easy to achieve, and I was very surprised compared with my experience of observing hospitals in Japan until then. However, for emergency diseases in which stroke or acute coronary syndrome is suspected, a flowing response has been established, and it was interesting that a system and communication network had been built to allocate specialist doctors and personnel to the patients who need them.

Overall, what I felt from doing the clerkship in Sweden is that the balance between work and private life is very good. Outpatient clinics and scheduled surgery end by 4 p.m., and on Fridays by 12 noon. Of course, after that there are emergency operations, paperwork and research, but even including them, I got the impression that the medical staff value not only work but also their private time and families. Especially regarding the outpatient clinic, in order to visit a highly specialized medical facility like the one where I did my clerkship, one must be referred through a neighborhood general practitioner or the like and be judged to need it, so it is precisely because the number of unnecessary visits can be reduced that the outpatient slots can be kept within hours. What was half shocking was that it is normal for doctor couples who both work full-time to have two or three children. What supports this situation includes systems outside medicine, such as an environment in which both spouses can take parental leave, well-developed public babysitting services and nurseries, and free education up to university. I thought I would very much like to take such systems and ways of thinking into Japan too. In addition, I also interacted with Japanese doctors working as graduate students at Lund University, and in the research field too they felt it was easier to work compared with Japan. In Sweden a personal number system has been established for many years, and medical information and so on are all managed according to this number. As a result, within the Skåne region, which has the same chart system, the charts of almost any hospital can be viewed, and transfers and referrals can be carried out smoothly. In addition, an attractive system had been built, such as being able to use the number to anonymously collect patient data necessary for clinical research.

Of course, on the other hand, I also reaffirmed the strengths of Japanese medicine, such as the prompt response in emergency departments and the shortness of the period from diagnosis of a disease until surgery. What I have described above is of course an opinion from the limited viewpoint of a student, so I would like to learn more deeply from now on about the system of Japan and of Nagoya University's medical departments, and about situations abroad. Through this study abroad, I felt that every healthcare system and welfare system has strengths and weaknesses, and that by comparing and combining them we can make something better, so I resolved that when I work as a doctor after graduation, I will broaden my perspective beyond medical knowledge and skills and contribute to further improvement of Japanese medicine.
